title: From fork() to Fleet: Designing an Agent Sandbox Cloud — Abhishek Bhardwaj, OpenAI
talk_summary: He then covers disk persistence via incremental block-level snapshots (copy-on-write + FIEMAP) and orchestration tricks like warm pools, memory-snapshot restore, and snapshot-locality scheduling.

takeaways.technique: MicroVM isolation for untrusted agent code
takeaways.what_they_do: Run agent tool execution inside hardware-virtualized microVMs (Cloud Hypervisor/Firecracker) rather than containers, so a guest kernel exploit cannot reach the host kernel; jail emulated devices individually.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Just please use micro VMs from the start. And then if it doesn't work, tell me and then we can talk about other things.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use copy-on-write writable layers over a base image, track changed blocks with FIEMAP, upload only the diff as an artifact, and restore by replaying the snapshot lineage onto the base image.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you call snapshot twice, I'm just snapshotting the diff between the two snapshots. Otherwise, if I have to save gigabytes of data at every turn, like like I'm going to bankrupt the company

takeaways.what_they_do: When restoring a sandbox from a multi-layer snapshot, route the request to the node that already holds the most layers, minimizing download.
takeaways.evidence_quote: node B has all the layers that you need. So, the scheduler then routes you and it it gives it the highest score and routes it because it has all the snapshot layers.

takeaways.technique: Warm pool + memory-snapshot restore for fast starts
takeaways.what_they_do: Pre-warm sandboxes or restore from a saved guest-memory snapshot in milliseconds, with a hybrid that grows a warm pool from memory snapshots to avoid idle CPU cost.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can actually take a memory snapshot of a micro VM and just-in-time start it start it in milliseconds as the request comes

takeaways.technique: Device jailing and seccomp on VMM backends
takeaways.what_they_do: Jail each emulated device (block, net) with only the permissions it needs, and use seccomp filters to shrink the kernel attack surface, so compromising one device doesn't own the node.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you attack the block device, we've only given it permission to access block resources. So, you can't access network resources.

takeaways.technique: Two-tier control plane (region cluster + node scheduler)
takeaways.what_they_do: A top-level control plane picks a cluster by region load and proximity to the harness, and an in-cluster scheduler picks a node by load and health, avoiding dying nodes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The scheduler tells you which node to pick based on the load and other factors, right? So, if nodes are dying or failing, it won't choose that.
